summary: Defines a way for Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) routers to deal with equal-cost multipaths. Using hash algorithms to choose among the paths does not allow traffic to be spread well, so this document adds a redirect mechanism. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When there are several equally good paths back to a multicast source, each router used to pick one by its own rule, and the operator had little control. This RFC lets the router at the source end tell the others which path to use.

questions: how does pim handle equal cost multipath
how does pim pick among equal cost paths
subtitle: Lets an upstream multicast router tell downstream routers which of several equal-cost paths to send traffic back along.

tldr.problem: When a multicast router has several equal-cost paths back to the source, it picks one by a local rule such as a hash of the addresses. The operator cannot spread the traffic by bandwidth or preference, and the pick differs from router to router.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6754 adds a PIM ECMP Redirect message. When an upstream router sees a Join or traffic on a path it does not want, it sends a Redirect naming the neighbour and interface it prefers, with a preference value and a metric to break ties.
tldr.outcome: Downstream routers send their Joins to the path the operator chose, and the control messages only appear when traffic needs rebalancing. The RFC is a Proposed Standard from October 2012, updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

today: RFC 6754 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2012. It is updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with Picking a Path by Hash
sections.content:
A PIM router uses the RPF procedure to select an upstream interface and a PIM neighbour on that interface to build forwarding state. When there are equal-cost multipaths upstream, existing implementations often use hash algorithms to select a path. Such algorithms do not allow the spread of traffic among the ECMPs according to administrative metrics, which usually leads to inefficient or ineffective use of network resources. This document introduces the ECMP Redirect, a mechanism to improve the RPF procedure over ECMP. It allows ECMP selection to be based on administratively selected metrics, such as data transmission delays, path preferences and routing metrics, or a combination of metrics.

ECMPs are frequently used in networks to provide redundancy and to increase available bandwidth, and a PIM router selects a path in the ECMP based on its own implementation-specific choice. The selection is a local decision: one way is to choose the PIM neighbour with the highest IP address, another is to pick the PIM neighbour with the best hash value over the destination and source addresses.

While implementations supporting ECMP have been deployed widely, the existing RPF selection methods have weaknesses. The lack of administratively effective ways to allocate traffic over alternative paths is a major issue. For example, there is no straightforward way to tell two downstream routers to select either the same or different RPF neighbour routers for the same traffic flows. With the ECMP Redirect mechanism, the upstream routers use a PIM ECMP Redirect message to instruct the downstream routers on how to break the tie among the upstream neighbours.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router was on its own when choosing between equal paths, so the operator could not say how much traffic should go each way. This RFC lets the upstream side make that choice for everyone.

sections.title: The Words Used Here
sections.content:
In this document, the term ECMP refers to parallel, single-hop, equal-cost links between adjacent nodes. An ECMP bundle is a set of PIM-enabled interfaces on a router where all interfaces belonging to the same bundle share the same routing metric, and the next hops for the ECMP are all one hop away. There can be one or more ECMP bundles on any router, while one individual interface can only belong to a single bundle, and ECMP bundles are created on a router by configuration.

RPF stands for Reverse Path Forwarding. Upstream means towards the root of the multicast forwarding tree; an upstream router is one that is forwarding, or potentially capable of forwarding, data packets onto interfaces in an ECMP bundle, and when multiple routers forward packets onto interfaces in the bundle, all of them are called upstream routers. Downstream means away from the root of the tree; a downstream router is one that uses an interface in the ECMP bundle as its RPF interface for a multicast forwarding entry.
sections.plainLanguage: An ECMP bundle is the group of parallel links a router has to the same place, all with the same cost. Routers above the bundle are upstream, routers below are downstream.

sections.title: How the Redirect Works
sections.content:
The existing PIM Assert mechanism allows the upstream router to detect the existence of multiple forwarders for the same multicast flow onto the same downstream interface. The upstream router sends a PIM Assert message containing a routing metric for the downstream routers to use for tiebreaking among the multiple upstream forwarders on the same RPF interface. With ECMP interfaces between the downstream and upstream routers, the ECMP Redirect mechanism works in a similar way but extends the ability to resolve the selection of forwarders among different interfaces in the ECMP.

When a PIM router downstream of the ECMP interfaces creates a new (*,G) or (S,G) entry, it populates the RPF interface and RPF neighbour information according to the rules specified by RFC 4601 and sends its initial PIM Joins to that RPF neighbour. When the RPF neighbour router receives the Join and finds that the receiving interface is one of the ECMP interfaces, it checks whether the same flow is already being forwarded out of another ECMP interface. If so, it sends a PIM ECMP Redirect message onto the interface the Join arrived on. The message contains the address of the desired RPF neighbour, an Interface ID, and the other parameters used as tiebreakers. In essence, a PIM ECMP Redirect message is sent by an upstream router to notify downstream routers to redirect PIM Joins to the new RPF neighbour via a different interface. When the downstream routers receive this message, they SHOULD trigger PIM Joins towards the new RPF neighbour specified in the packet.

The message has similar functions to the existing PIM Assert message: it is sent by an upstream router, it is used to influence the RPF selection by downstream routers, and a tiebreaker metric is used. The difference is that the Assert message selects an upstream router within the same multi-access network such as a LAN, while the Redirect message selects both a network and an upstream router. One advantage of this design is that the control messages are only sent when there is a need to rebalance the traffic, which reduces the amount of control traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: When a downstream router joins a group through a path the upstream router does not want, the upstream router replies with a message naming the path it prefers, and the downstream router joins that one instead.

sections.title: Sending an ECMP Redirect
sections.content:
ECMP Redirects are sent by an upstream router in a rate-limited fashion under either of two conditions: it detects a PIM Join on a non-desired outgoing interface, or it detects multicast traffic on a non-desired outgoing interface. In both cases the Redirect is sent to the non-desired interface. An outgoing interface is considered non-desired when the upstream router is already forwarding the same flow out of another interface belonging to the same ECMP bundle, or when it is not yet forwarding the flow out of any interface of the bundle but another interface has more desired attributes. An upstream router MAY choose not to send ECMP Redirects if it becomes aware that some of the downstream routers are unreachable via some links in the bundle.

The upstream router uses the Neighbor Address or the Interface ID field in the message to indicate the interface it wants traffic directed to. This Neighbor Address MUST be associated with an interface in the same ECMP bundle as the message's outgoing interface. If the Interface ID field is ignored, the Neighbor Address uniquely identifies a LAN and an upstream router to which a downstream router SHOULD redirect its Join messages, and the message MUST be discarded if the Neighbor Address does not match the cached neighbour address.

The Interface ID field is used in IPv4 when one or more RPF neighbours in the bundle are unnumbered, or in IPv6 where link-local addresses are in use. For other IPv4 usage this field is zeroed when sent and ignored when received, and if the Router ID part of the Interface ID is zero, the field MUST be ignored. If the Interface ID is not ignored, the receiving router MUST use it instead of the Neighbor Address to identify the new RPF neighbour, and the message MUST be discarded if the Interface ID does not match the cached Interface ID.
sections.plainLanguage: An upstream router sends the Redirect only when it sees a Join or traffic on a path it would rather not use, and it rate-limits these messages. The message names either the neighbour address or, where addresses are not usable, an interface identifier.

sections.title: Receiving a Redirect and Transient Failures
sections.content:
When a downstream router receives an ECMP Redirect and detects that the desired RPF path from its upstream router's point of view is different from its current one, it should join the newly suggested path and prune from the current path; the exact order of those actions is implementation specific. If a downstream router receives multiple ECMP Redirects sent by different upstream routers, it SHOULD use the Preference, Metric or other fields as tiebreakers to choose the most preferred RPF interface and neighbour. The tiebreak procedure is the same as that used in PIM Assert processing. If an upstream router receives an ECMP Redirect, it SHOULD NOT change its forwarding behaviour even if the message makes it a less preferred RPF neighbour.

During a transient network outage with a single link cut in an ECMP bundle, a downstream router may lose connection to its RPF neighbour and the normal operation may be interrupted. The downstream router SHOULD select a new RPF neighbour, preferring, among all ECMP upstream routers, the one on the LAN that the previous RPF neighbour resided on. If there is no upstream router reachable on that LAN, the router will select a new RPF neighbour on a different LAN, preferring the one that served as RPF neighbour before the link failure. Such a router can be identified by the Router ID, which is part of the Interface ID in the PIM ECMP Redirect Hello option.
sections.plainLanguage: On receiving a Redirect the downstream router joins the new path and gives up the old one. If a link breaks mid-way, it prefers to fall back to a router on the same network as the one it lost, then to the router that had served it before.

sections.title: Making Sure Everyone Speaks It
sections.content: If a PIM router supports this specification, it MUST send the PIM ECMP Redirect Hello Option in its PIM Hello messages. A PIM router sends ECMP Redirects on an interface only when it detects that all neighbours on that interface have sent this Hello option. If a PIM router detects that any of its neighbours on an ECMP bundle does not support this Hello option, it SHOULD NOT send ECMP Redirects to interfaces in that bundle; however, it SHOULD still process any ECMP Redirects received from interfaces in that same bundle. A PIM router that does not support this specification will ignore the PIM ECMP Redirect Hello Options and the ECMP Redirects in the PIM packets that it receives.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router announces in its regular hello that it understands this message. A router only sends Redirects on a link where every neighbour has announced support, but it will still act on Redirects it receives.

sections.title: The Message on the Wire
sections.content:
The PIM ECMP Redirect Hello Option has a Type of 32 and a Length of 0.

The ECMP Redirect message itself carries the PIM version, a Type of 11, reserved bits and a checksum as in RFC 4601, followed by a Group Address of 64 or 160 bits in the Encoded-Group format, a Source Address of 48 or 144 bits in the Encoded-Unicast format, a Neighbor Address of 32 or 128 bits that is the address of the desired upstream neighbour where the downstream receiver redirects its PIM Joins, and an Interface ID of 64 bits.

The Preference field is 8 bits and is the first tiebreaker when Redirects from multiple upstream routers are compared against each other; a numerically smaller value is preferred. A reserved value of 15 indicates that the metric value following the Preference field is a Network Time Protocol timestamp, encoded as in RFC 5905, taken at the moment the sending router started to forward out of this interface. The Metric field is 64 bits and is the second tiebreaker if the Preference values are the same, again with a numerically smaller value preferred; it can contain path parameters defined by users. When the Preference and Metric values are the same, the Neighbor Address or Interface ID field is used as the third tiebreaker, depending on which field identifies the RPF neighbour, and the bigger value wins.
sections.plainLanguage: The message names the group, the source, the neighbour to use, and two numbers that decide between competing messages: a small preference value first, then a metric.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security of the ECMP Redirect is only guaranteed by the security of the PIM packet, and the security considerations for PIM Assert packets as described in RFC 4601 apply here. Spoofed ECMP Redirect packets may cause the downstream routers to send PIM Joins to an undesired upstream router and trigger more ECMP Redirect messages. The security considerations for PIM packets described in RFC 4601 also apply to the new Hello option defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: The message has no protection of its own. Anyone who can forge PIM packets can send a Redirect and move traffic to a router of their choosing.

messages.label: PIM JOIN
messages.note: Sent on an interface the upstream router does not want to use.

messages.label: ECMP REDIRECT
messages.note: Names the desired RPF neighbour, plus a preference and metric.

messages.label: PIM JOIN
messages.note: Repeated toward the newly suggested neighbour.

fields.name: PIM Ver and Type
fields.desc: The PIM version and the message type, which is 11 for an ECMP Redirect.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: The PIM checksum, as in RFC 4601.

fields.name: Neighbor Address
fields.desc: The desired upstream neighbour, 32 or 128 bits.

fields.name: Interface ID
fields.desc: Used instead of the neighbour address where addresses are not usable.

fields.name: Preference
fields.desc: First tiebreaker; a smaller value is preferred. The value 15 means the metric is an NTP timestamp.

fields.name: Metric
fields.desc: Second tiebreaker; a smaller value is preferred.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The PIM Hello option type assigned to this option.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the option, which is zero.
